tasks.routeTitle: Ratios of subtriangle areas and cancellation around the triangle
tasks.currentSketch: Suppose AD, BE, CF concur at P. Since triangles PBD and PCD share the altitude from P to BC, [PBD]/[PCD]=BD/DC; analogously [PCE]/[PAE]=CE/EA and [PAF]/[PBF]=AF/FB. The product of these three area ratios is 1: express each area using two sides through P and their included angle; each factor cancels cyclically. Conversely, if the product is 1, two cevians meet at P and the same area-ratio identity forces the third through P. This is the area form of Ceva.

tasks.routeTitle: barycentric coordinates and a determinant condition
tasks.currentSketch: Use homogeneous barycentric coordinates A=(1,0,0), B=(0,1,0), C=(0,0,1), with D=(0:d₁:d₂) on BC, E=(e₁:0:e₂) on CA, F=(f₁:f₂:0) on AB. The line equations AD, BE, CF have coefficient rows (0,−d₂,d₁), (e₂,0,−e₁), (−f₂,f₁,0). Their determinant vanishes exactly when d₂e₁f₂=d₁e₂f₁, i.e. BD/DC·CE/EA·AF/FB=1. A zero determinant is exactly concurrency (with boundary/parallel degeneracies interpreted projectively).

tasks.entryDescription: Gaussian integer factorization; Wilson's theorem and factorial congruences; lattice-point/continued-fraction arguments.
tasks.currentSketch: For prime p≡1 mod4, Wilson gives (p−1)!≡−1. Pair k with p−k for 1≤k≤(p−1)/2 to rewrite (p−1)!≡(−1)^((p−1)/2)(((p−1)/2)!)²; since (p−1)/2 is even, this produces a square root of −1 modulo p. In Gaussian integers, p divides (x+i)(x−i); gcd factors and unique factorization yield p=a²+b². The Wilson congruence alone gives modular square root, not yet integer sum-of-squares.

tasks.entryDescription: Gaussian integer factorization; Wilson's theorem and factorial congruences; lattice-point/continued-fraction arguments.
tasks.currentSketch: Since −1 is a square mod p, choose t with t²≡−1 (mod p). The lattice Λ={(a,b)∈Z²:a≡tb (mod p)} has determinant p. Minkowski’s convex body theorem applied to a disk of radius just below √(2p) gives a nonzero lattice point with 0<a²+b²<2p. The congruence implies p|(a²+b²), hence a²+b²=p. For p>2 the vector cannot have both coordinates divisible by p because its norm²<p². This is a geometry-of-numbers proof and depends on Minkowski’s theorem.

tasks.entryDescription: Gauss's lemma and lattice-point parity; Eisenstein's lattice-point proof; Jacobi sums/Gaussian sums. *Proofs from THE BOOK* includes distinct proofs.
tasks.currentSketch: For distinct odd primes p,q, Gauss's lemma says (q/p)=(-1)^N where N counts least positive residues of q,2q,…,((p−1)/2)q that exceed p/2. Counting lattice points in the rectangle 1≤i≤(p−1)/2, 1≤j≤(q−1)/2 below/above the line qi=pj gives N_p+N_q=((p−1)/2)((q−1)/2), yielding (p/q)(q/p)=(-1)^(((p−1)/2)((q−1)/2)).

tasks.entryName: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic for polynomials over a field
tasks.entryDescription: Euclidean algorithm/induction on degree; factorization in the PID F[x]; algebraic closure and root splitting.
tasks.currentSketch: For nonzero f,g∈F[x], divide f=qg+r with deg r<deg g. Repeated division terminates by strict degree descent and yields gcd as a linear combination; irreducibles are prime by Bézout, and induction on degree gives factorization and uniqueness up to nonzero constants/order.

tasks.entryDescription: Euclidean algorithm/induction on degree; factorization in the PID F[x]; algebraic closure and root splitting.
tasks.currentSketch: In an algebraic closure, repeatedly split any reducible polynomial into lower-degree factors until every factor is irreducible; degree strictly decreases, guaranteeing termination. Uniqueness follows because F[x] is a PID and irreducibles there are prime. Algebraic closure is unnecessary for the existence factorization and this route is therefore not as independent as it first appears.

tasks.routeTitle: Expand logarithmic derivative of the generating polynomial
tasks.currentSketch: Write P(t)=∏(1+x_i t)=∑e_k t^k. Then tP'(t)/P(t)=∑_{m≥1}(-1)^{m-1}p_m t^m, where p_m=∑x_i^m. Multiply by P and compare t^k coefficients to obtain Newton's recurrence.

tasks.currentSketch: For a permutation, power sums encode choices of a distinguished cycle while elementary symmetric functions encode sets of distinct labels; splitting permutations by the cycle containing a chosen label gives the same recurrence, with sign from cycle length. This is a combinatorial interpretation, not a third independent algebraic identity.

tasks.routeTitle: Möbius inversion on the Boolean lattice
tasks.currentSketch: On the subset lattice define (φf)(T)=Σ_{Y⊇T}f(Y). Define ψ by (ψf)(T)=Σ_{Y⊇T}(−1)^{|Y−T|}f(Y). In φψ, the coefficient of f(Z) is Σ_{T⊆Y⊆Z}(−1)^{|Y−T|}=(1−1)^{|Z−T|}, equal to 1 for Z=T and 0 otherwise. Thus ψ=φ⁻¹, giving Boolean-lattice Möbius inversion and inclusion–exclusion.
